topics.name: Displacement Current and the Ampere-Maxwell Law
topics.summary: Ampere's original law, \( \oint\vec B\cdot d\vec l=\mu_0I_c \), fails for a charging capacitor: a surface cutting the wire encloses current, but a surface passing between the plates encloses none. Maxwell fixed this by adding the displacement current \( I_d=\epsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt} \), which arises from a changing electric flux and involves no motion of charge. The Ampere-Maxwell law is \( \oint\vec B\cdot d\vec l=\mu_0(I_c+I_d) \). Between the plates, \( I_c=0 \) but \( I_d \) is non-zero, and in a simple charging circuit \( I_d \) equals the wire current exactly at every instant, so the total current is continuous. Displacement current is a genuine source of magnetic field: a changing electric field produces a magnetic field, just as a changing magnetic field produces an electric field. When the capacitor is fully charged, the field stops changing and \( I_d=0 \). This symmetry is what makes electromagnetic waves possible.
key_formulas: \( I_d=I_c \) in a simple charging circuit
topics.worked_example:
A capacitor with plate area 0.1 m\( ^{2} \) and separation 1 mm has its voltage rising at \( 10^{6} \) V/s. Find \( I_d \).

\( C=\dfrac{(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.1)}{10^{-3}}=8.85\times10^{-10} \) F.

\( I_d=C\dfrac{dV}{dt}=8.85\times10^{-4} \) A, equal to the current in the wires.
common_mistakes: Using only \( I_c \) (the unmodified law) for a surface between the plates, getting zero.
Treating \( I_d \) and \( I_c \) as unrelated; in a charging circuit they are exactly equal.
Thinking displacement current is charge jumping across the gap.
Using the flux itself instead of its rate of change.

topics.name: Nature of Electromagnetic Waves: Transverse Character, Phase Relationship, and Speed
topics.summary: An electromagnetic wave consists of oscillating electric and magnetic fields that regenerate each other and travel through vacuum without any medium. The wave is purely transverse: \( \vec E \) and \( \vec B \) are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel, which is along \( \vec E\times\vec B \) (never \( \vec B\times\vec E \), which is the opposite direction). The two fields oscillate in phase, reaching their maximum and zero values at the same place and instant; a \( 90^\circ \) lag is an AC-circuit idea that does not apply here. Their magnitudes are related by \( E=cB \) at every instant, so \( E_0/B_0=c \). The speed in vacuum is \( c=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}}=3\times10^{8} \) m/s for every frequency and wavelength. Frequency and wavelength are linked by \( c=f\lambda \), and angular frequency and wave number by \( \omega=ck \).
key_formulas: Direction of travel along \( \vec E\times\vec B \)
topics.worked_example:
A wave has \( E_0=300 \) V/m, with \( \vec E \) along \( +\hat i \) and \( \vec B \) along \( +\hat j \).

\( B_0=\dfrac{300}{3\times10^{8}}=10^{-6} \) T.

Direction: \( \hat i\times\hat j=\hat k \), so the wave travels along \( +\hat k \).
common_mistakes: Giving \( E \) and \( B \) a \( 90^\circ \) phase difference.
Using \( \vec B\times\vec E \) and getting the reversed direction.
Believing higher-frequency waves travel faster in vacuum.

topics.name: Energy Density, Intensity, and Radiation Pressure of Electromagnetic Waves
topics.summary: Electromagnetic waves carry energy and momentum. The electric energy density is \( u_E=\tfrac12\epsilon_0E^2 \) and the magnetic energy density is \( u_B=\dfrac{B^2}{2\mu_0} \). Because \( E=cB \) and \( c^2=\dfrac{1}{\mu_0\epsilon_0} \), these are always exactly equal, so each field carries half the energy. Averaging over a cycle, the total average energy density is \( u_{avg}=\tfrac12\epsilon_0E_0^2 \), and the intensity is \( I=u_{avg}c=\tfrac12\epsilon_0cE_0^2 \), proportional to the square of the amplitude. Energy \( U \) carries momentum \( U/c \), so waves exert radiation pressure. For a fully absorbing surface, \( P=\dfrac{I}{c} \); for a perfectly reflecting surface, \( P=\dfrac{2I}{c} \), because the momentum reverses, like an elastic ball bouncing off a wall. Pressure depends on intensity only, not on frequency, and force equals pressure times area.
topics.worked_example:
Light of intensity 1200 W/m\( ^{2} \) falls on a perfectly reflecting mirror.

\( P=\dfrac{2I}{c}=\dfrac{2400}{3\times10^{8}}=8\times10^{-6} \) Pa.

If the surface absorbed instead, the pressure would be half: \( 4\times10^{-6} \) Pa.
common_mistakes: Using \( I/c \) for a reflecting surface, or \( 2I/c \) for an absorbing one.
Thinking the electric or magnetic energy dominates; they are equal.
Forgetting the \( \tfrac12 \) or the square in \( I=\tfrac12\epsilon_0cE_0^2 \).
Thinking higher-frequency radiation exerts more pressure at the same intensity.

topics.name: The Electromagnetic Spectrum: Wavelength and Frequency Ranges
topics.summary: All electromagnetic waves are the same kind of wave, differing only in frequency and wavelength, and all travel at \( c \) in vacuum. In order of increasing frequency (decreasing wavelength) the spectrum is: radio waves (longer than 0.1 m), microwaves (0.1 m to 1 mm), infrared (1 mm to 700 nm), visible light (700 nm to 400 nm), ultraviolet (400 nm to 1 nm), X-rays (1 nm to \( 10^{-3} \) nm) and gamma rays (below \( 10^{-3} \) nm). This order is fixed. Energy per photon increases with frequency, so shorter wavelength means higher photon energy: a gamma photon carries far more energy than a radio photon. To identify a band from a frequency, first convert using \( \lambda=\dfrac{c}{f} \), then compare the wavelength with the ranges. Keep the neighbours straight: microwaves sit between radio and infrared, and ultraviolet sits between visible and X-rays.
key_formulas: Order: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma
topics.worked_example:
Identify the band of a wave of frequency \( 1.5\times10^{15} \) Hz.

\( \lambda=\dfrac{3\times10^{8}}{1.5\times10^{15}}=2\times10^{-7} \) m \( =200 \) nm.

200 nm lies between 400 nm and 1 nm, so it is ultraviolet.
common_mistakes: Placing X-rays before ultraviolet, or microwaves after infrared.
Thinking longer wavelength means more energy per photon.
Thinking gamma rays or X-rays travel faster than radio waves in vacuum.
Forgetting unit conversions (nm, \( \mu\text{m} \), cm) before comparing ranges.

topics.name: Production, Detection, and Applications of Electromagnetic Waves Across the Spectrum
topics.summary: Each band has characteristic sources, detectors and uses. Radio waves come from accelerated charges in oscillating circuits and antennas and are used for communication. Microwaves are produced by klystron and magnetron valves and used in radar and microwave ovens, where their frequency matches water molecules in food. Infrared is emitted by warm and hot bodies and molecules; it is used in remote controls and thermal imaging, and trapped infrared causes the greenhouse effect. Visible light comes from electron transitions in atoms and is detected by the eye and photographic film. Ultraviolet comes from very hot bodies such as the Sun and special lamps; it is detected by photocells, used for sterilization, and mostly absorbed by the ozone layer. X-rays come from high-energy electrons striking a metal target and are used in medical diagnosis and crystallography. Gamma rays come from nuclear transitions in radioactive decay and are used in cancer treatment.
key_formulas: Infrared: warm bodies; remote controls, thermal imaging, greenhouse effect
Ultraviolet: very hot bodies, lamps; sterilization; absorbed by ozone
X-rays: electrons hitting metal; diagnosis, crystallography
topics.worked_example:
A hospital images a fracture and then treats a tumour.

Fracture imaging uses X-rays, produced by fast electrons hitting a metal target.

Tumour treatment uses gamma rays, from nuclear transitions, which lie at even higher frequency.
common_mistakes: Confusing X-ray production (electrons on metal) with gamma production (nuclei).
Linking the greenhouse effect to ultraviolet instead of infrared.
Thinking remote controls use microwaves.
Thinking the ozone layer absorbs infrared rather than ultraviolet.

questions.topic: Displacement Current and the Ampere-Maxwell Law
questions.question: Which statement correctly describes displacement current?
options: It arises from a changing electric flux and involves no actual motion of charge.
It is a flow of electrons that jumps across the gap between capacitor plates.
It arises from a changing magnetic flux through a surface.
It exists only when the electric field stays constant in time.
questions.explanation:
Maxwell defined displacement current as \( I_d=\epsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt} \).

It depends only on how fast the electric flux changes; no charge physically moves through the region.

Even so, it produces a magnetic field exactly like an ordinary current.
questions.hint: Look at what changes in the gap of a charging capacitor: charges or the electric field?
distractor_logic: Confuses displacement current with conduction current; no charge crosses the insulating gap.
A changing magnetic flux induces an emf (Faraday's law); displacement current comes from changing electric flux.
A constant electric field gives zero rate of change of flux, so the displacement current would be zero.

questions.topic: Displacement Current and the Ampere-Maxwell Law
questions.question: Which expression gives the displacement current \( I_d \) through a surface?
questions.explanation:
Displacement current is proportional to the RATE of change of electric flux.

The constant of proportionality is the permittivity of free space: \( I_d=\epsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt} \).

Check: \( \epsilon_0 \) times V m/s works out to C/s, which is ampere.
questions.hint: A current is a rate, so the formula must contain a time derivative.
distractor_logic: Uses the magnetic constant \( \mu_0 \) instead of the permittivity \( \epsilon_0 \).
Uses the flux itself rather than its rate of change; a steady flux gives no displacement current.
Divides by \( \epsilon_0 \) instead of multiplying, which does not give units of current.

questions.topic: Displacement Current and the Ampere-Maxwell Law
questions.question: Which is the correct form of the Ampere-Maxwell law?
questions.explanation:
Maxwell added the displacement current to the conduction current as a source of magnetic field.

The law becomes \( \oint\vec B\cdot d\vec l=\mu_0(I_c+I_d) \), with \( I_d=\epsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt} \).

This makes the total current continuous everywhere, including across a capacitor gap.
questions.hint: Maxwell did not remove the conduction current; he added something to it.
distractor_logic: This is the original, unmodified Ampere's law, which fails where conduction current is discontinuous.
Subtracts the displacement current; both currents act as sources of \( \vec B \) and add.
Uses \( \epsilon_0 \) as the constant in front; Ampere's law uses \( \mu_0 \).

questions.topic: Displacement Current and the Ampere-Maxwell Law
questions.question: Who introduced the idea of displacement current to correct Ampere's circuital law?
questions.explanation:
Maxwell noticed that Ampere's law gives contradictory results for a charging capacitor.

He fixed it by adding the displacement current term \( \epsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt} \).

This correction led him to predict electromagnetic waves.
questions.hint: The same scientist predicted electromagnetic waves theoretically.
distractor_logic: Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction (changing magnetic flux), not displacement current.
Hertz experimentally produced and detected electromagnetic waves after Maxwell's prediction.
Ampere gave the original law that needed the correction; he did not add the extra term.

questions.topic: Displacement Current and the Ampere-Maxwell Law
questions.question: A capacitor is being charged by a battery. What is the conduction current in the empty gap between its plates?
options: Equal to the current in the connecting wires
Twice the current in the connecting wires
Half the current in the connecting wires
questions.explanation:
Conduction current needs charges to move, but the gap between the plates is empty.

So \( I_c=0 \) in the gap.

What does exist there is a displacement current, because the electric field between the plates is changing.
questions.hint: Can electrons actually travel through the empty space between the plates?
distractor_logic: This value belongs to the displacement current in the gap, not the conduction current.
No charge flows across the gap, so nothing can double the wire current there.
The gap is an insulator; there is no partial flow of charge across it.

questions.topic: Displacement Current and the Ampere-Maxwell Law
questions.question: In a simple circuit where a capacitor is being charged, how does the displacement current between the plates compare with the conduction current in the wires at the same instant?
options: The displacement current is always zero.
The displacement current is always smaller.
They are unrelated and can take any values.
questions.explanation:
The charge on the plate is \( Q=\epsilon_0 EA \), so \( \dfrac{dQ}{dt}=\epsilon_0\dfrac{d(EA)}{dt}=\epsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt} \).

The left side is the wire current \( I_c \) and the right side is \( I_d \).

Hence \( I_d=I_c \) at every instant, keeping the total current continuous.
questions.hint: The rate at which charge piles up on the plate controls how fast the field between the plates grows.
distractor_logic: Ignores the changing electric field between the plates, which gives a non-zero \( I_d \).
Assumes some current is lost in the gap; in fact \( I_d=I_c \) exactly at every instant.
Treats \( I_d \) and \( I_c \) as independent; the same charge build-up fixes both, so they must match.

questions.topic: Displacement Current and the Ampere-Maxwell Law
questions.question: Can displacement current produce a magnetic field?
options: No, it produces only an electric field.
Only if it flows inside a metal conductor.
Yes, it produces a magnetic field in the same way as a conduction current.
Only after the capacitor becomes fully charged.
questions.explanation:
In the Ampere-Maxwell law, \( I_d \) sits next to \( I_c \) as a source of \( \vec B \).

So a changing electric field produces a magnetic field, even in empty space.

This is exactly how the magnetic field between capacitor plates arises.
questions.hint: Look at where \( I_d \) appears in the Ampere-Maxwell law.
distractor_logic: Denies the central point of Maxwell's correction: \( I_d \) is a genuine source of \( \vec B \).
Displacement current exists even in vacuum; no conductor is needed.
When fully charged, the field stops changing, so \( I_d \) becomes zero.

questions.topic: Displacement Current and the Ampere-Maxwell Law
questions.question: A capacitor has become fully charged and the voltage across it no longer changes. What is the displacement current between its plates now?
options: Equal to the initial charging current
Equal to \( \epsilon_0 \) times the electric field
questions.explanation:
\( I_d=\epsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt} \).

When the voltage is steady, the field and flux between the plates are constant.

So \( \dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt}=0 \) and \( I_d=0 \).
questions.hint: Is anything changing between the plates once charging is complete?
distractor_logic: The displacement current is largest while the field changes fastest, not when it has stopped changing.
The initial charging current has died out; with no change in field there is no \( I_d \).
Uses the field itself rather than its rate of change; \( I_d \) needs a changing flux.

questions.topic: Nature of Electromagnetic Waves: Transverse Character, Phase Relationship, and Speed
questions.question: In an electromagnetic wave, how are the electric field, the magnetic field, and the direction of propagation oriented?
options: The electric field is along the direction of propagation.
The electric and magnetic fields are parallel to each other.
The magnetic field is along the direction of propagation.
questions.explanation:
An electromagnetic wave is purely transverse.

\( \vec E \) is perpendicular to \( \vec B \), and both are perpendicular to the direction of travel.

The travel direction is along \( \vec E\times\vec B \).
questions.hint: EM waves are transverse. What does that say about each field?
distractor_logic: Would make the wave partly longitudinal; EM waves have no field component along propagation.
\( \vec E \) and \( \vec B \) are always perpendicular to each other in an EM wave.
Would give a longitudinal magnetic component; \( \vec B \) is transverse too.

questions.topic: Nature of Electromagnetic Waves: Transverse Character, Phase Relationship, and Speed
questions.question: What is the phase relationship between the electric and magnetic fields in an electromagnetic wave travelling through vacuum?
questions.explanation:
In a travelling EM wave, \( E \) and \( B \) reach their maximum and zero values at the same place and instant.

So \( E=cB \) holds at every instant, not just for amplitudes.

A \( 90^\circ \) lag belongs to AC circuit quantities, not to the fields of a wave.
questions.hint: Does \( E \) become zero at the same moment that \( B \) does?
distractor_logic: Carries over the phase lag from LCR circuits; in an EM wave there is no lag.
Same false carryover from AC circuits, just with the lag reversed.
Opposite phase would reverse the sign of \( \vec E\times\vec B \) every half cycle; the fields actually peak together.

questions.topic: Nature of Electromagnetic Waves: Transverse Character, Phase Relationship, and Speed
questions.question: The direction of propagation of an electromagnetic wave is along
questions.explanation:
The propagation direction is given by the cross product \( \vec E\times\vec B \), in that order.

Since \( \vec B\times\vec E=-\vec E\times\vec B \), swapping the order reverses the direction.

It is perpendicular to both fields, consistent with a transverse wave.
questions.hint: Order matters in a cross product.
distractor_logic: Reverses the cross-product order, which points in exactly the opposite direction.
The wave is transverse, so it cannot travel along its own electric field.
The wave is transverse, so it cannot travel along its own magnetic field.

questions.topic: Nature of Electromagnetic Waves: Transverse Character, Phase Relationship, and Speed
questions.question: For an electromagnetic wave in vacuum, the ratio of the electric field amplitude to the magnetic field amplitude, \( E_0/B_0 \), equals
questions.explanation:
For an EM wave in vacuum, \( E_0=cB_0 \).

So \( \dfrac{E_0}{B_0}=c=3\times10^{8} \) m/s.

This is why the magnetic field amplitude in tesla is tiny compared with the electric field in V/m.
questions.hint: Check units: V/m divided by T gives m/s.
distractor_logic: Squares the speed; the relation is \( E_0=cB_0 \), not \( E_0=c^2B_0 \).
Inverts the ratio; \( 1/c \) is \( B_0/E_0 \).
\( \mu_0\epsilon_0 \) equals \( 1/c^2 \), not \( c \).

questions.topic: Nature of Electromagnetic Waves: Transverse Character, Phase Relationship, and Speed
questions.question: The speed of electromagnetic waves in vacuum is given by
questions.explanation:
Maxwell's equations give \( c=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}} \).

Putting in the values gives about \( 3\times10^{8} \) m/s.

This matched the measured speed of light, showing light is an EM wave.
questions.hint: Remember \( c^2=1/(\mu_0\epsilon_0) \).
distractor_logic: Forgets the reciprocal; \( \sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0} \) is \( 1/c \).
Forgets the square root; \( 1/(\mu_0\epsilon_0) \) equals \( c^2 \).
This ratio has units of resistance (the impedance of free space), not speed.

questions.topic: Nature of Electromagnetic Waves: Transverse Character, Phase Relationship, and Speed
questions.question: Electromagnetic waves are
options: transverse in the magnetic field but longitudinal in the electric field
questions.explanation:
Both \( \vec E \) and \( \vec B \) oscillate perpendicular to the direction of propagation.

So an electromagnetic wave is purely transverse.
questions.hint: Compare the directions of the fields with the direction of travel.
distractor_logic: Longitudinal waves vibrate along the travel direction; EM fields are perpendicular to it.
Neither field has any component along the propagation direction.
Both fields are perpendicular to the direction of travel; neither is longitudinal.

questions.topic: Nature of Electromagnetic Waves: Transverse Character, Phase Relationship, and Speed
questions.question: Do electromagnetic waves need a material medium to travel?
options: Yes, they need air or some other gas.
Yes, they need a solid medium.
No, they can travel through vacuum.
They travel only through conducting materials.
questions.explanation:
An EM wave consists of electric and magnetic fields that regenerate each other.

Fields exist in empty space, so no material medium is needed.

Sunlight crossing space is the everyday proof.
questions.hint: How does sunlight reach the Earth?
distractor_logic: Light reaches us from the Sun through empty space, so no gas is needed.
Confuses EM waves with mechanical waves like sound in solids.
Conductors actually tend to absorb or reflect EM waves; vacuum is ideal for travel.

questions.topic: Nature of Electromagnetic Waves: Transverse Character, Phase Relationship, and Speed
questions.question: An electromagnetic wave in vacuum has frequency \( 10^{6} \) Hz. Taking \( c=3\times10^{8} \) m/s, what is its wavelength?
questions.explanation:
Use \( c=f\lambda \), so \( \lambda=\dfrac{c}{f} \).

\( \lambda=\dfrac{3\times10^{8}}{10^{6}}=300 \) m.
questions.hint: Wavelength equals speed divided by frequency.
distractor_logic: Multiplies \( c \) by \( f \) instead of dividing.
Drops one power of ten while dividing.
Divides \( f \) by \( c \), which inverts the correct relation.

questions.topic: Energy Density, Intensity, and Radiation Pressure of Electromagnetic Waves
questions.question: The energy density of the electric field in an electromagnetic wave is
questions.explanation:
The electric energy density is \( u_E=\tfrac12\epsilon_0E^2 \), the same formula used for a capacitor.

It depends on the square of the field.
questions.hint: Recall the energy stored per unit volume in a capacitor's field.
distractor_logic: Drops the factor \( \tfrac12 \); \( \epsilon_0E^2 \) is the total (electric plus magnetic) energy density.
Forgets to square the field; energy density goes as \( E^2 \).
Divides by \( \epsilon_0 \) instead of multiplying; this does not give J/m\( ^{3} \).

questions.topic: Energy Density, Intensity, and Radiation Pressure of Electromagnetic Waves
questions.question: The energy density of the magnetic field in an electromagnetic wave is
questions.explanation:
The magnetic energy density is \( u_B=\dfrac{B^2}{2\mu_0} \), the same as inside an inductor.

Note the \( \mu_0 \) is in the denominator.
questions.hint: Think of the energy stored per unit volume in a solenoid.
distractor_logic: Multiplies by \( \mu_0 \) instead of dividing, copying the electric formula's pattern incorrectly.
Forgets to square \( B \).
Drops the factor \( \tfrac12 \).

questions.topic: Energy Density, Intensity, and Radiation Pressure of Electromagnetic Waves
questions.question: In an electromagnetic wave, how does the electric energy density \( u_E \) compare with the magnetic energy density \( u_B \) at any instant?
options: \( u_B \) is much larger than \( u_E \)
questions.explanation:
\( u_E=\tfrac12\epsilon_0E^2 \) and \( u_B=\dfrac{B^2}{2\mu_0} \).

Put \( E=cB \): \( u_E=\tfrac12\epsilon_0c^2B^2 \).

Since \( \epsilon_0c^2=\dfrac{1}{\mu_0} \), this equals \( \dfrac{B^2}{2\mu_0}=u_B \). The two are always equal.
questions.hint: Substitute \( E=cB \) and use \( c^2=1/(\mu_0\epsilon_0) \).
distractor_logic: Mixes up the field ratio \( E=cB \) with the energy-density ratio, which is 1.
Tiny values of \( B \) in tesla mislead; \( B^2/\mu_0 \) balances exactly.
Forgets that \( c^2=1/(\mu_0\epsilon_0) \) cancels the factor completely.

questions.topic: Energy Density, Intensity, and Radiation Pressure of Electromagnetic Waves
questions.question: An electromagnetic wave of intensity \( I \) falls normally on a surface that absorbs it completely. The radiation pressure is
questions.explanation:
Energy \( U \) carries momentum \( U/c \).

For full absorption, momentum per second per unit area is \( I/c \), which is the pressure.

So \( P=\dfrac{I}{c} \).
questions.hint: When absorbed, the wave's momentum is simply handed over to the surface.
distractor_logic: This is the pressure on a perfectly reflecting surface, not an absorbing one.
Multiplies by \( c \); pressure is intensity divided by speed.
Divides by \( c^2 \); that is the formula pattern for mass-energy, not pressure.

questions.topic: Energy Density, Intensity, and Radiation Pressure of Electromagnetic Waves
questions.question: An electromagnetic wave of intensity \( I \) falls normally on a perfectly reflecting surface. The radiation pressure is
questions.explanation:
On reflection, momentum \( p \) becomes \( -p \), so the change is \( 2p \).

This is like an elastic ball bouncing back from a wall.

So \( P=\dfrac{2I}{c} \), double the absorbing value.
questions.hint: Compare a ball that sticks to a wall with one that bounces back.
distractor_logic: This is for an absorbing surface; reflection reverses the momentum and doubles the transfer.
Halves instead of doubling the absorbing value.
Doubles twice; the momentum change on reflection is exactly twice, not four times.

questions.topic: Energy Density, Intensity, and Radiation Pressure of Electromagnetic Waves
questions.question: The intensity \( I \) of an electromagnetic wave is related to its average energy density \( u_{avg} \) by
questions.explanation:
Intensity is energy crossing unit area per second.

In one second, the energy in a column of length \( c \) passes through, so \( I=u_{avg}\,c \).
questions.hint: How far does the wave's energy travel in one second?
distractor_logic: Divides by \( c \); energy flow rate needs multiplication by the speed.
Squares the speed; the units would not be W/m\( ^{2} \).
Ignores that energy moves at speed \( c \); J/m\( ^{3} \) is not W/m\( ^{2} \).

questions.topic: Energy Density, Intensity, and Radiation Pressure of Electromagnetic Waves
questions.question: Why does an electromagnetic wave exert pressure on a surface it falls on?
options: Because the wave's electric field repels the surface's electrons outward.
Because the wave carries momentum as well as energy.
Because the wave heats the surface and the air pushes on it.
questions.explanation:
An EM wave carrying energy \( U \) also carries momentum \( U/c \).

When this momentum is absorbed or reversed at a surface, a force acts on it.

Force per unit area is the radiation pressure.
questions.hint: A force needs a rate of change of something.
distractor_logic: EM waves carry momentum \( U/c \) without any rest mass.
The pressure comes from momentum transfer, not an electrostatic repulsion.
Radiation pressure exists even in vacuum with no air present.

questions.topic: Energy Density, Intensity, and Radiation Pressure of Electromagnetic Waves
questions.question: The intensity of an electromagnetic wave is proportional to
options: the reciprocal of its electric field amplitude
the square root of its electric field amplitude
the square of its electric field amplitude
questions.explanation:
\( I=\tfrac12\epsilon_0cE_0^2 \).

So intensity grows as the square of the field amplitude: doubling \( E_0 \) makes \( I \) four times larger.
questions.hint: Energy density contains \( E^2 \).
distractor_logic: Forgets that energy density depends on \( E^2 \), not \( E \).
A stronger field carries more energy, not less.
Inverts the power dependence.

questions.topic: The Electromagnetic Spectrum: Wavelength and Frequency Ranges
questions.question: Which sequence lists the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing frequency?
options: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays
Radio waves, infrared, microwaves, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays
Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible, X-rays, ultraviolet, gamma rays
Gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves, radio waves
questions.explanation:
Frequency increases (wavelength decreases) in this fixed order: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma.

Any swap of neighbours breaks the canonical sequence.
questions.hint: Start from the longest wavelength and move toward the shortest.
distractor_logic: Swaps microwaves and infrared; microwaves have lower frequency than infrared.
Places X-rays before ultraviolet; ultraviolet has lower frequency than X-rays.
This is the order of decreasing frequency (increasing wavelength), the reverse of what is asked.

questions.topic: The Electromagnetic Spectrum: Wavelength and Frequency Ranges
questions.question: Which part of the electromagnetic spectrum has the shortest wavelength?
questions.explanation:
Gamma rays sit at the high-frequency end of the spectrum.

Highest frequency means shortest wavelength, below about \( 10^{-3} \) nm.
questions.hint: Shortest wavelength is at the highest-frequency end.
distractor_logic: Radio waves have the longest wavelength, not the shortest.
Ultraviolet lies well before X-rays and gamma rays in the sequence.
X-rays are the second shortest; gamma rays lie beyond them.

questions.topic: The Electromagnetic Spectrum: Wavelength and Frequency Ranges
questions.question: Which part of the electromagnetic spectrum has the longest wavelength?
questions.explanation:
Radio waves are at the low-frequency end, with wavelengths greater than about 0.1 m.

Lowest frequency means longest wavelength.
questions.hint: Longest wavelength is at the lowest-frequency end.
distractor_logic: Microwaves come next after radio waves; their wavelength is shorter.
Infrared wavelengths are well below a millimetre, much shorter than radio.
Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength of all.

questions.topic: The Electromagnetic Spectrum: Wavelength and Frequency Ranges
questions.question: What is the approximate wavelength range of visible light?

questions.topic: The Electromagnetic Spectrum: Wavelength and Frequency Ranges
questions.question: Which carries more energy per photon: infrared or ultraviolet radiation?

It depends only on the brightness of the source
questions.explanation:
Photon energy increases with frequency, so it increases as wavelength decreases.

Ultraviolet has shorter wavelength than infrared, so each ultraviolet photon carries more energy.
questions.hint: Shorter wavelength means higher frequency.

Photon energy depends on frequency, which differs between the two bands.

questions.topic: The Electromagnetic Spectrum: Wavelength and Frequency Ranges
questions.question: Which band of the electromagnetic spectrum lies between visible light and X-rays?

questions.topic: The Electromagnetic Spectrum: Wavelength and Frequency Ranges
questions.question: In vacuum, which of these electromagnetic waves travels the fastest?
options: All travel at the same speed
questions.explanation:
Every electromagnetic wave travels at \( c=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}} \) in vacuum.

This does not depend on frequency or wavelength.
questions.hint: Does the formula for \( c \) contain frequency?
distractor_logic: Higher frequency or energy does not mean higher speed in vacuum.
Longer wavelength does not mean higher speed in vacuum.
Visible light has no special speed; every EM wave moves at \( c \) in vacuum.

questions.topic: Production, Detection, and Applications of Electromagnetic Waves Across the Spectrum
questions.question: Which electromagnetic waves are used for cooking food in ovens?
questions.explanation:
Microwave ovens use microwaves whose frequency is matched to water molecules in food.

The molecules absorb energy and the food heats up.
questions.hint: The appliance is named after the waves.
distractor_logic: Infrared heats surfaces (as in a grill) but is not what a microwave oven uses.

questions.topic: Production, Detection, and Applications of Electromagnetic Waves Across the Spectrum
questions.question: A television remote control usually sends signals using

distractor_logic: Microwaves are used for radar, ovens and some communication links, not typical remotes.

questions.topic: Production, Detection, and Applications of Electromagnetic Waves Across the Spectrum
questions.question: Which radiation is used to kill germs and sterilize surgical instruments?

questions.topic: Production, Detection, and Applications of Electromagnetic Waves Across the Spectrum
questions.question: Which radiation is used by doctors to detect bone fractures?
questions.explanation:
X-rays pass through soft tissue but are absorbed more by bone.

This contrast produces an image of the skeleton, used in medical diagnosis.
questions.hint: The radiograph you get at a hospital.
distractor_logic: Gamma rays are used mainly for treating cancer, not for routine fracture imaging.
Infrared is used in thermal imaging, not for seeing bones.
Microwaves are used in radar and ovens.

questions.topic: Production, Detection, and Applications of Electromagnetic Waves Across the Spectrum
questions.question: Which radiation is emitted during radioactive decay of nuclei?

Ultraviolet comes from very hot bodies and special lamps.

questions.question: The ozone layer in the atmosphere absorbs most of the Sun's

questions.topic: Displacement Current and the Ampere-Maxwell Law
questions.question: Charge on a capacitor plate increases at a steady rate of 2 mA while it is being charged. What is the displacement current between the plates?

So \( I_d=2 \) mA, exactly equal to the wire current.
questions.hint: The displacement current equals the rate at which charge builds up on a plate.

questions.question: A parallel-plate capacitor has plate area 0.1 m\( ^{2} \) and plate separation 1 mm. Its voltage rises at \( 10^{6} \) V/s. With \( \epsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12} \) C\( ^{2} \)/(N m\( ^{2} \)), find the displacement current.

questions.topic: Displacement Current and the Ampere-Maxwell Law
questions.question: A capacitor is discharging through a resistor. At some instant the current in the wires is 3 A. What is the magnitude of the displacement current between the plates at that instant?
options: It cannot be found without the plate area
questions.explanation:
During discharge the field between the plates decreases, so \( \dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt} \) is non-zero.

In magnitude, \( I_d=\left|\dfrac{dQ}{dt}\right|=I_c=3 \) A.

Only the sense reverses compared with charging.
questions.hint: The equality \( I_d=I_c \) holds whether the charge is increasing or decreasing.
distractor_logic: Assumes the gap carries no current of any kind during discharge.
Doubles the value by counting both plates.
Area is not needed; \( I_d \) must equal the wire current in magnitude.

questions.question: The electric flux through a surface between the plates of a capacitor changes at \( 10^{9} \) V m/s. With \( \epsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12} \) C\( ^{2} \)/(N m\( ^{2} \)), what is the displacement current through that surface?
questions.hint: Apply the definition directly.
distractor_logic: Ignores the rate of change of flux and gives only \( \epsilon_0 \).

questions.topic: Displacement Current and the Ampere-Maxwell Law
questions.question: A capacitor with circular plates is being charged. Loop P encircles the connecting wire; loop Q, identical in size and larger than the plates, encircles the gap between the plates. How does \( \oint\vec B\cdot d\vec l \) around Q compare with that around P?
options: It is twice as large around Q.
questions.explanation:
Around P: enclosed current is the conduction current \( I \).

Around Q: enclosed current is the displacement current, and \( I_d=I \).

So both line integrals equal \( \mu_0I \).
questions.hint: Which current passes through each loop, and how are they related?
distractor_logic: Uses the unmodified Ampere's law with only conduction current, which is zero in the gap.
No mechanism doubles the current in the gap; \( I_d \) equals the wire current.
The wire carries a real conduction current, so the integral around P is certainly non-zero.

questions.topic: Displacement Current and the Ampere-Maxwell Law
questions.question: A current of 4 A flows in the wires charging a capacitor. A surface is chosen that passes through the gap between the plates without touching any wire. In the Ampere-Maxwell law, what are the conduction current and the displacement current through this surface?
questions.explanation:
The surface cuts no wire, so no charge flows through it: \( I_c=0 \).

The electric field in the gap is changing, so \( I_d=I=4 \) A.

The total \( I_c+I_d=4 \) A, the same as for a surface cutting the wire.
questions.hint: Ask separately: does charge cross this surface, and does electric flux through it change?
distractor_logic: Swaps the two: no charge crosses the gap, so \( I_c \) there must be zero.
Double counts; the surface misses the wire, so it has only displacement current.
Ignores the changing field in the gap, which gives a displacement current.

questions.question: In an electromagnetic wave, at a certain point the electric field is along \( +\hat i \) and the magnetic field is along \( +\hat j \). In which direction does the wave travel?

\( \hat i\times\hat j=\hat k \).

questions.topic: Nature of Electromagnetic Waves: Transverse Character, Phase Relationship, and Speed
questions.question: An electromagnetic wave in vacuum has angular frequency \( 6\times10^{9} \) rad/s. Taking \( c=3\times10^{8} \) m/s, find its wave number \( k \).
questions.explanation:
For an EM wave in vacuum, \( \omega=ck \).

\( k=\dfrac{\omega}{c}=\dfrac{6\times10^{9}}{3\times10^{8}}=20 \) rad/m.
questions.hint: Wave speed equals \( \omega/k \).
distractor_logic: Multiplies \( \omega \) by \( c \) instead of dividing.
Divides \( c \) by \( \omega \), inverting the relation.
Adds a stray factor of \( \pi \) while converting between \( \omega \) and \( k \).

questions.topic: Nature of Electromagnetic Waves: Transverse Character, Phase Relationship, and Speed
questions.question: An electromagnetic wave travels along \( +\hat k \) and its electric field at some point is along \( +\hat i \). Along which direction is its magnetic field at that point?
questions.explanation:
We need \( \vec E\times\vec B \) along \( +\hat k \) with \( \vec E \) along \( +\hat i \).

Since \( \hat i\times\hat j=\hat k \), \( \vec B \) is along \( +\hat j \).
questions.hint: Which unit vector, crossed after \( \hat i \), gives \( \hat k \)?
distractor_logic: Gives \( \vec E\times\vec B \) along \( -\hat k \), the wrong way.

\( E \) and \( B \) oscillate in phase.

questions.question: At a particular point and instant, the electric field of an electromagnetic wave in vacuum is 150 V/m. Taking \( c=3\times10^{8} \) m/s, what is the magnetic field there at that same instant?
questions.explanation:
Because the fields are in phase, \( E=cB \) holds at every instant, not only for amplitudes.

\( B=\dfrac{150}{3\times10^{8}}=5\times10^{-7} \) T.
questions.hint: The relation \( E=cB \) works for instantaneous values too.

questions.topic: Energy Density, Intensity, and Radiation Pressure of Electromagnetic Waves
questions.question: Sunlight of intensity 900 W/m\( ^{2} \) falls normally on a surface that absorbs it completely. Taking \( c=3\times10^{8} \) m/s, find the radiation pressure.

Divides by \( c^2 \) instead of \( c \).

questions.question: A beam of intensity 1200 W/m\( ^{2} \) falls normally on a perfectly reflecting mirror. Taking \( c=3\times10^{8} \) m/s, find the radiation pressure on the mirror.

For full reflection, \( P=\dfrac{2I}{c} \).

\( P=\dfrac{2(1200)}{3\times10^{8}}=8\times10^{-6} \) Pa.

The average of \( \sin^2 \) is \( \tfrac12 \), so average electric energy density is \( \tfrac14\epsilon_0E_0^2 \), and magnetic is the same.
